name: SAMMA

lead: SAMMA is a polymer made from mandelic acid, the same acid used in gentle skincare peels.
It was developed as a vaginal microbicide and contraceptive candidate, so appearance uses refer to mandelic acid itself rather than SAMMA.

paras: It blocks HIV and HSV from attaching to cells by targeting viral envelope proteins, and disrupts sperm acrosome function.
Only laboratory and preclinical studies exist; it is not a marketed product.

angle.text: SAMMA is not a skin product; people interested in mandelic acid for skin texture and pigmentation use the monomer in peels, while the polymer has been studied for infection prevention.

lead: SAMMA is a mandelic acid condensation polymer, a compound derived from mandelic acid, the alpha hydroxy acid used in skincare peels.[1] SAMMA itself was developed as a candidate vaginal microbicide, not a cosmetic, and is included here because of its link to mandelic acid chemistry.
Laboratory work reported that SAMMA blocks HIV and herpes simplex virus from binding to cells with little cytotoxicity, and it was licensed for development as a contraceptive microbicide.[2][3]

paras: A 2002 study reported that SAMMA was highly effective against HIV isolates in primary human cells and inhibited herpes simplex infection by targeting viral envelope proteins.[2] A study of dendritic cell-mediated HIV transmission followed in 2007.[4] A separate study found that SAMMA induces premature acrosome loss in human sperm through calcium signalling, relevant to its contraceptive aim.[3]

Mandelic acid is an aromatic alpha hydroxy acid discovered in 1831 and used in superficial chemical peels considered suitable across skin types; a 2022 review lists 40% mandelic acid among agents that improve pigmentation and texture, while the American Academy of Dermatology says evidence is insufficient to recommend peels for acne.[1]
No studies found. Published SAMMA work is laboratory and preclinical.

timeline.event: SAMMA reported as a candidate HIV and HSV microbicide.[2]
